lesson.title: Reading the Shape of a Relationship
lesson.summary: Scatterplots reveal how two quantitative variables relate, and describing one well means naming its direction, form, and strength together, in context.
lesson.body:
A scatterplot is the first tool statisticians reach for whenever they want to study how two quantitative variables move together. Each point on the graph represents one individual, plotted using its pair of measurements, one value read off the horizontal axis and one off the vertical axis. When one of the two variables might plausibly explain changes in the other, it is conventional to place that one on the horizontal axis, a habit that becomes important once regression lines enter the picture. Before calculating anything at all, a careful look at the cloud of points already tells a real story, and learning to describe that story in words is a skill of its own, one that has to come before any formula.

Three features, taken together, give a complete description of a scatterplot. Direction asks whether the variables tend to rise together, a positive association, or whether one tends to fall as the other rises, a negative association. Form asks what shape the overall pattern traces out: a straight line, a curve, distinct clusters, or no discernible pattern at all. Strength asks how closely the individual points hug that form, from tightly bunched around a clear trend to loosely scattered with only a faint hint of a pattern. A useful scatterplot description also notes anything that breaks from the main pattern, such as a lone point sitting far from the rest of the cloud, since a single unusual point can change the whole impression a graph gives.

Form deserves special attention because it decides which tools apply later. A relationship can be strong without being linear, and the methods covered in the next several chapters, correlation and least squares regression, are built specifically to summarize straight line patterns. Calling a curved relationship linear just because it happens to be strong is a common and consequential mistake, so form is always checked before it is assumed, ideally by imagining whether a single straight line, rather than a bent or curved one, would trace through the middle of the cloud reasonably well.

Consider five students, with hours spent studying for an exam and the score they earned: 1 hour and 50 points, 2 hours and 60 points, 3 hours and 65 points, 4 hours and 80 points, and 5 hours and 90 points. Plotting these five points shows a clear upward drift, so the direction is positive: more studying goes with higher scores. The points fall close to a straight line rather than curving, so the form is linear. Four of the five points sit almost exactly on a rising line, with only the 3 hour, 65 point student dipping slightly below where the pattern would predict, so the overall strength is strong, since one modest deviation among five points still leaves a tight, consistent trend.

A full, useful description ties all three features together in context rather than listing them separately: there is a strong, positive, linear association between hours studied and exam score. That single sentence, grounded in the actual variables rather than generic symbols, is far more informative than the scatterplot alone, and it sets up exactly what the next chapters will measure precisely: how strong is strong, expressed as an exact number, and what specific line best captures that trend for making predictions.
